theme: Lift up your heads, O gates, the King of glory enters
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 24. Read it as a processional song, with questions and answers. Picture the ark being carried up to the city, and the gates opening to receive the King.
settingTheScene: You read Psalm 24 earlier, in Unit 6, as part of the story of the temple and God’s presence. Here it appears again, in its natural setting after the ark’s arrival in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). It is likely the very song sung when David brought the ark up to Zion. Today, read it with that scene in mind, and notice how it moves from the whole earth to a single hill, and from the hill to the King who enters.
observation: “The earth is the LORD’s and the fullness thereof, the world and those who dwell therein” (v. 1).
“For he has founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers” (v. 2).
“Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD? And who shall stand in his holy place?” (v. 3).
“He who has clean hands and a pure heart, who does not lift up his soul to what is false” (v. 4).
“He will receive blessing from the LORD and righteousness from the God of his salvation” (v. 5).
“Lift up your heads, O gates! And be lifted up, O ancient doors, that the King of glory may come in!” (v. 7).
“Who is this King of glory? The LORD, strong and mighty, the LORD, mighty in battle!” (v. 8).
“Who is this King of glory? The LORD of hosts, he is the King of glory!” (v. 10).
interpretation:
The psalm has three movements, and the second reading adds a layer to each. First, a declaration: the whole earth belongs to the LORD. He made it and holds it together. The God who has come to Zion is not a local deity. He is the Creator of all. When David brought the ark to Jerusalem, he was bringing the throne of the God of the whole earth.

Second, a question: “Who shall ascend the hill of the LORD?” Having just read of Uzzah, the question is sharp. Not everyone can approach God in any way they like. The answer is a person of clean hands and a pure heart, whose actions and desires are right. But no one fits that description perfectly. The question hangs over the reader, and it prepares for the good news that someone has fulfilled it.

Third, a procession. The company reaches the gates of the city and calls on them to open. The call-and-response is dramatic: “Who is this King of glory?” The answer comes: “The LORD, strong and mighty.” Then the call is made again, and the answer is expanded: “The LORD of hosts.” The king who comes is the commander of the heavenly armies.

Having read the account of the ark’s arrival, we see how the psalm fits. The ark, a symbol of God’s throne, is brought into the city. But no gate in Jerusalem could finally contain him. The psalm points beyond the ark to the day when the King of glory would truly enter the city.

The key move is from the heights to the humble. The one who owns the whole earth comes to a particular hill. The one who is infinitely holy invites sinners to come near, if they are clean. The gospel is that he makes us clean.
connection: Jesus is the one with clean hands and a pure heart, the only one who can ascend the hill of the LORD. He entered Jerusalem as King (Matthew 21:9), and he ascended into heaven, where the gates are lifted for him (Hebrews 4:14; Ephesians 4:8-10). We ascend with him by faith, clothed in his righteousness (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 10:19-22). Paul quotes verse 1 in 1 Corinthians 10:26.
application:
Thank God that your access to him does not depend on your clean hands, but on Christ’s.

Look at how you treat what you have. If the earth is the LORD’s, so are your possessions.

Open the gates of your heart to the King of glory today.
prayerPrompts: Open a gate in your life for the King of glory, and name it.
Thank Jesus, who ascended with clean hands and clothes you in his righteousness.
Praise God that the earth and everything in it is his.
